title: Do auto technicians need EPA Section 609 certification to service vehicle air conditioning?
description: EPA Section 609 rules for motor vehicle air conditioning: who needs certification under 40 CFR 82.34, program standards in 82.40 and 3 year shop records.
shortAnswer: Yes. Under 40 CFR 82.34, the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) prohibits anyone repairing or servicing motor vehicle air conditioners for payment from performing any service involving the refrigerant unless they are trained and certified by an EPA-approved Section 609 program under 40 CFR 82.40 and use approved equipment. Anyone servicing off-road MVAC-like systems must be certified even when not paid. Shops must certify their equipment to EPA and keep records for three years.
keyTakeaways: Section 609 certification applies to service involving refrigerant on motor vehicle air conditioners (MVACs) done for consideration, meaning paid in cash, credit, goods or services. Top-offs count as service involving refrigerant.
MVAC-like appliances, such as air conditioning on agricultural or construction vehicles, may be serviced by technicians certified under either Section 609 or Section 608 Type II.

Approved programs must train through on-the-job, self-study or instructor-led means, test on service standards and environmental effects, use independent grading, verify identity, and issue each technician a unique number.
Section 609 certification has no expiry date in the rule; EPA reserves the right to require recertification in future.
Service shops must certify to EPA that they own approved equipment and that every authorized user is certified, and must keep the supporting records on site for at least three years.
regulator: US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), under section 609 of the Clean Air Act
appliesTo: Persons who repair or service motor vehicle air conditioners for consideration, including dealerships, independent repair shops, fleet operators and quick-service outlets
Persons who repair or service MVAC-like appliances on off-road vehicles and equipment, paid or not
Owners of refrigerant recovery and recycling equipment used for MVAC service
Sellers of small containers of class I or class II MVAC refrigerant, and organizations running Section 609 training and certification programs

blocks.text: Anyone repairing or servicing MVACs for consideration, and anyone repairing or servicing MVAC-like appliances, must be properly trained and certified before performing any service involving the refrigerant. The prohibition is in [40 CFR 82.34(a)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/40/82.34), which also requires proper use of equipment approved under section 82.36.

The definitions in [40 CFR 82.32](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/40/82.32) do most of the work. Service for consideration means being paid to perform service, whether in cash, credit, goods or services, and includes all service except that done for free. Service involving refrigerant means any service during which release of refrigerant can reasonably be expected, and expressly includes a top-off where the system is charged and nothing else is done. Refrigerant includes class I and class II substances and, since November 15, 1995, any substitute.

An MVAC is mechanical vapor compression refrigeration equipment that cools the driver's or passenger's compartment of a motor vehicle. Under [40 CFR 82.152](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/40/82.152), an MVAC-like appliance is an open-drive compressor appliance with a full charge of 20 pounds or less used to cool the compartment of off-road vehicles or equipment, including agricultural and construction vehicles. For MVAC-like work the paid or unpaid distinction does not apply, and either Section 609 or Section 608 Type II certification is accepted.

blocks.title: Currency
blocks.text: This page reflects 40 CFR 82.34, 82.40 and 82.42 as published in the Electronic Code of Federal Regulations as at November 2026. Section 82.40 was last amended at 86 FR 15595 (March 24, 2021). EPA updated its list of approved Section 609 programs on November 2, 2026.

sections.heading: What must an approved Section 609 training program include?

blocks.text: Section 609 programs are run by EPA-approved organizations, not by EPA itself. [40 CFR 82.40(a)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/40/82.40) sets four standards a program must meet to be approved.

items: **Training:** adequate training through one or more of on-the-job training, self-study of instructional material, or on-site training with instructors, videos or hands-on demonstration.

**Test subject material:** the service and repair standards in section 82.36(a) and appendices A to F to Subpart B (refrigerant containment, extraction and recycling equipment, and refrigerant purity), anticipated technology changes, the environmental consequences of refrigerant release and ozone depletion, and the requirements imposed under section 609.

**Test administration:** completed tests graded by an entity or individual who receives no benefit from the outcome, measures at the test site to ensure honest completion, and a means of verifying the test taker's identity. Where a translator is used, the certificate must say so.
**Proof of certification:** individual proof such as a certificate, wallet card or display card, and a unique number for each certified technician.

blocks.text: Approved programs must also review their test material periodically against the latest technology in MVAC service and submit a written summary of the review and any changes to EPA every two years under section 82.40(c). EPA's [Section 609 programs page](https://www.epa.gov/mvac/section-609-technician-training-and-certification-programs) lists approved programs, including some intended only for the sponsoring organization's own employees.

The rule sets no expiry. Section 82.40(d) states that the Administrator reserves the right to specify the need for technician recertification at some future date, which means a valid card issued by an approved program remains valid unless EPA acts.

Certification can be lost. Under section 82.40(f), EPA's authorized representatives may require technicians to demonstrate, on the business premises, proper recovery and recycling procedures. Failure to demonstrate or to use the equipment properly may lead to revocation, and a technician whose certification is revoked must be recertified before servicing any MVAC.

EPA's programs page also tells refrigerant retailers to continue accepting cards from a list of organizations that formerly ran Section 609 programs, which confirms that older cards remain valid when the issuing program closes. A lifetime credential still leaves room for knowledge drift; the guide on [detecting outdated training content](/guides/how-to-detect-outdated-training-content) applies to shop-level refreshers.

sections.heading: What must a repair shop certify and record?

blocks.text: A shop servicing MVACs for consideration must certify to EPA that it has acquired and is properly using approved equipment and that each person authorized to use it is properly trained and certified. Under [40 CFR 82.42(a)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/40/82.42), the certification is a signed statement by the equipment owner or a responsible officer giving the purchaser's name, the establishment address, and the equipment manufacturer, model, manufacture date and serial number, sent to the EPA regional office for the shop's state.

Section 82.42(b) requires owners of approved recycling equipment to keep records demonstrating that all persons authorized to operate it are currently certified under section 82.40, and records of where recovered refrigerant is sent where applicable. All records must be kept for at least three years, and shops servicing MVACs for consideration must keep them on site and give EPA inspectors access.

In practice that means a copy of every technician's card, linked to the equipment they are authorized to use, kept at the shop. The guide on [how long to keep training records](/guides/how-long-to-keep-training-records) discusses aligning retention across rules with different periods.

sections.heading: Who can buy small cans of vehicle refrigerant?

blocks.text: Containers of less than 20 pounds of class I or class II MVAC refrigerant may be sold only to persons trained and certified under section 82.40, or to buyers who certify in writing that the containers are for resale only. This restriction has applied since November 15, 1992 under section 82.34(b).

Sellers must verify that the purchaser is certified, keep the records for three years, and display a sign stating: "It is a violation of federal law to sell containers of Class I and Class II refrigerant of less than 20 pounds of such refrigerant to anyone who is not properly trained and certified to operate approved refrigerant recycling equipment."

For substitute refrigerants such as HFC-134a, the Subpart F sales restriction applies instead. EPA's [Section 608 regulatory updates page](https://www.epa.gov/section608/regulatory-updates-section-608-refrigerant-management-regulations) explains that small cans of 2 pounds or less of non-exempt substitutes for MVAC servicing can be sold without technician certification if they have a self-sealing valve.

sections.heading: How do Section 609 duties map to roles and evidence?

blocks.text: A vehicle service shop carries most Section 609 duties at business level, not only through its technicians. This page-specific grid shows the owner of each duty, its timing, and the documents an EPA inspector would reasonably ask for under sections 82.34 to 82.42.

blocks.text: A shop running several sites can hold these as one register, as described in [preparing training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry maps the Section 609 test subjects, such as containment practice, equipment use and refrigerant purity, to concepts and assessment points, and links each technician record to the equipment they are authorized to operate. That makes the shop's three year certified operator record a by-product of the framework rather than a separate file.

faqs.q: Do I need Section 609 certification to recharge my own car?
faqs.a: Section 82.34(a) applies to persons servicing MVACs for consideration, so unpaid work on your own vehicle is outside the certification requirement. Separate rules still apply to buying refrigerant: class I and class II refrigerant in containers under 20 pounds can only be sold to certified technicians, and substitute small cans must meet the self-sealing valve conditions.

faqs.q: Can a Section 608 certified technician service car air conditioning?
faqs.a: Not for passenger compartment MVACs serviced for consideration, which require Section 609 certification under 40 CFR 82.161(a)(1)(vi) and 82.34. Section 608 Type II certification is accepted for MVAC-like appliances on off-road vehicles and equipment.

faqs.q: Is a Section 609 test open book?
faqs.a: Section 82.40 does not prescribe a closed-book format. It requires independent grading, measures at the test site to ensure tests are completed honestly, and identity verification, leaving the format to each approved program within those standards.

faqs.q: Does a shop that only does refrigerant top-offs need certified technicians?
faqs.a: Yes. Section 82.32 defines service involving refrigerant to include a top-off, and states that facilities performing only top-offs are subject to all requirements that apply to facilities doing a wider range of refrigerant service, including approved equipment and certified technicians.
